chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
title: Sitting in at sessions and how it has become harder
summary: Sitting in has gone on since the music began; now players ask whether you can play, and standards rose after the early Thirties.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: You know, something that's still not quite clear to me is about, you know, playing sessions, just the musicians sitting in and things like that. That started pretty early in the game?
Oh, that's been going on, I guess, since they started playing Jazz, I suppose.
There would always be some place where you could go after work and play.

Yes. If guys were with a band that ...(?)..., they'd sit in -- to keep their chops up, you know. But now, when you go to sit in, the guys want to know "Can you play?" You have to be sure you can play something.
You mean it was more informal then? Now it's...?
Dickenson - 149
Yeah, than it is now.
Well, now you also run into things like people saying, 'Well, we have our own arrangements' and things...

Yeah. It's ....(?). That nixes them from... Unless they know them. If they know them, they let them come and sit in -- or somebody knows them in the band. It's getting harder, a little harder for guys to come and sit in today than it was in those days.
Is that also because there are more different ways of playing?
Yes, it is. Yes.
Did that come about sort of after Bebop came in?
No. It was... I guess maybe around that time. I guess so. Maybe. They were getting a little choosy in the Thirties. During the Twenties and the early Twenties, all right, you know. But...
Was that also maybe because musicians became more accomplished...?
Yeah, I think so.
...and the standards were higher?
I think so. I would think so.
Sometimes when you listen to some of the older records, you can see that some guys might have problems with playing the right harmony and changes and so on. Not that you don't
Dickenson - 150
still get that sometimes. But was that more of a common problem in the earlier days? I suppose you might always have at least a couple of guys in the band that didn't come up to...
What they called the standards, right?
Right. Or were there a lot of good musicians then, too?
